answer.answer: We prove the identity by expanding the determinant in the columns and then recognizing the single-column-replacement terms as adjugate entries. Let the columns of A be a_1,...,a_n. The rank-one matrix u v^T has columns v_1 u,...,v_n u, so the columns of A+u v^T are a_i+v_i u. By multilinearity of det in each column, det(A+u v^T) expands as det(A) plus the sum of terms in which one column a_i is replaced by v_i u, plus terms with at least two replaced columns. A term with at least two replaced columns has two linearly dependent columns (multiples of u), so it vanishes by the alternating property. Hence det(A+u v^T)=det(A)+Σ_{i=1}^n v_i det(A^{(i)}), where A^{(i)} is A with column i replaced by u. Now expand det(A^{(i)}) along column i. If C_{j,i}=(-1)^{j+i} det(A with row j and column i deleted), with the empty minor convention det(empty)=1, then det(A^{(i)})=Σ_{j=1}^n C_{j,i} u_j. The classical adjugate is defined by (adj(A))_{i,j}=C_{j,i}; therefore (adj(A)u)_i=Σ_{j=1}^n C_{j,i}u_j=det(A^{(i)}). Thus Σ_i v_i det(A^{(i)})=Σ_i v_i(adj(A)u)_i=v^T adj(A)u. Combining gives det(A+u v^T)=det(A)+v^T adj(A)u. This argument never divides by det(A) and never uses A^{-1}, so it is valid for every n>=1 and every A, singular or not. For every n>=1 and every n by n matrix A over a commutative field R, including singular A, det(A+u v^T)=det(A)+v^T adj(A)u. Singular matrices are included in this identity, so C20.singular_included is true. If A is invertible, the adjugate satisfies adj(A)=det(A)A^{-1}. Substituting into the general identity gives det(A+u v^T)=det(A)+v^T(det(A)A^{-1})u=det(A)(1+v^T A^{-1}u). The invertibility hypothesis is needed only for this rewriting: it supplies A^{-1} and lets det(A) be factored out. When A is singular, A^{-1} does not exist and det(A)=0, so the factored expression is not available, even though the adjugate identity remains true.

derivation_steps.statement: Let the columns of A be a_1,...,a_n. Since u v^T has columns v_1 u,...,v_n u, the columns of A+u v^T are a_i+v_i u for i=1,...,n.

By multilinearity of det in columns, det(A+u v^T) equals the sum over subsets S of {1,...,n} of (product_{i in S} v_i) times det(B_S), where B_S has column i equal to u for i in S and equal to a_i otherwise.
For |S|>=2, choose two distinct i,j in S; the columns i and j of B_S are both u, hence identical, so det(B_S)=0 by the alternating property.
Thus only S empty and singletons remain: det(A+u v^T)=det(A)+sum_{i=1}^n v_i det(A^{(i)}), where A^{(i)} is A with column i replaced by u.
Define the cofactor C_{j,i}=(-1)^{j+i} times the determinant of A with row j and column i deleted, using det(empty)=1 so that for n=1, C_{1,1}=1 and adj([a])=[1].
Expanding det(A^{(i)}) along its i-th column u gives det(A^{(i)})=sum_{j=1}^n C_{j,i} u_j.
With the classical adjugate defined by (adj(A))_{i,j}=C_{j,i}, we have (adj(A)u)_i=sum_{j=1}^n C_{j,i}u_j=det(A^{(i)}).
Therefore sum_{i=1}^n v_i det(A^{(i)})=sum_{i=1}^n v_i (adj(A)u)_i=v^T adj(A)u.
Combining the previous equalities gives det(A+u v^T)=det(A)+v^T adj(A)u, with no division by det(A) and no use of A^{-1}, so the identity holds for every n>=1 and every A, singular or not.
If A is invertible, adj(A)=det(A)A^{-1}; substituting into the general identity yields det(A+u v^T)=det(A)+v^T(det(A)A^{-1})u=det(A)(1+v^T A^{-1}u).

The invertibility hypothesis is needed only for this rewriting: it supplies A^{-1} and allows det(A) to be factored out. If A is singular, A^{-1} does not exist and det(A)=0, so the factored expression is unavailable, while the adjugate identity remains valid.
